doc.title: John Beal interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2024

title: Philip Glass
summary: Beal jammed with Glass at Juilliard, later played film scores and a Beckett piece with him, and found repetitive music hard to record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Philip Glass was in Juilliard when I was there and he liked to jam. He had a house in Chinatown that he paid $65 a month rent. It was like a pretty, frame house, ramshackle, and we’d play down there once in a while. I had a motorcycle and I went down with the

bass on a motorcycle and we would play down there. And then later on you know what happened with him, he got very big. I played a couple of film scores with him, played some incidental music for a Beckett play that he wrote for tympani and double bass. And Beckett had instructed that there be no music for this play, I forget the name of the play. So he wrote tympani and bass. I guess that’s not music. But talking about technology and recording you know, his style is repetitive phrases, repetitive with slight variations. So recording is like really tough and you have to go back and punch in and the repetitions — it was very hard to keep track of that stuff you know.
Yeah. Okay, play this measure 80 times.
Well not 80, but maybe four bars four times and then eight bars six times, you know, with like slight differences you know. But you know, a very popular style.
I was watching a video of his music — I can’t pronounce this, “Koyaanisqatsi.” I think you might have played on that. Sound familiar?
That’s all right. I think it’s pretty standard with you fellows to say, “Oh you played on that, don’t you remember?” I remember Bucky did that a number of times.
